chapter_theme: Refusing flesh (புலால் மறுத்தல்): those who eat flesh are thrown into hell, and those who give up killing, theft, lust and lying and reach Siva's feet are free of them in the bliss of knowledge.

199.reading: Those vile ones who eat foul flesh are seized by Yama's messengers in sight of all, flung on their backs into fire-mouthed hell and broken.
199.nuance: புலையர், a word for the lowest outcastes, is used here for flesh-eaters, so baseness is a matter of what one eats rather than one's birth. செல்லாக in the third line is obscure: 'as they go', or perhaps 'like a thunderbolt'; the sense of the verse doesn't depend on it.

200.reading: Killing, theft, lust and lying are sins as great as mountains; those who give them up, reach Siva's feet, which are the highest, and the joy there, have none of these, and that is the holy state of the bliss of knowledge.
200.nuance: The chapter is on refusing flesh, but this verse widens it to a list of great sins in which killing comes first and flesh-eating is not named. The last line makes freedom from the sins a mark of the state reached, not only a precondition for it.

links.note: Both send the flesh-eater to hell; the Kural says hell's mouth will not open to let him out, Tirumular describes his being flung into fire-mouthed hell.
Both make eating creatures a deed that returns on the eater; the Naladiyar's crab-eater gets a wasting disease in a later life, Tirumular's flesh-eater hell.
